answer: Paying 1 point to go from 7% to 6.75% cuts the payment by $16.7 per $100,000 borrowed, so the point takes 59.9 months (about five years) to pay for itself. Across 2,635 start weeks of the weekly 30-year rate since April 1971, the market rate fell at least 1.25 points (enough to make a refinance from 6.75% worthwhile by the common one-point rule) before that break-even in 53.1% of weeks; when it did, the median wait was 18.9 months. Restricting to weeks that started between 6.5% and 7.5% (362 weeks) gives 52.2%. The latest weekly rate is 7.03%. History, not a forecast.
guess: Buyers are usually told points pay off if you keep the loan past break-even, so they would picture a borrower who stays put five years and expect the point to pay off most of the time.
changesDecision: In roughly half of history, a refinance-sized drop arrived before the point had paid for itself, usually within a couple of years, which would leave part of the point unrecovered. Whether to pay the point therefore depends on whether the buyer would refinance in that case, not only on how long they plan to live in the home.

assumptions: One point costs 1% of the loan and lowers the rate by 0.25 (7.00% to 6.75%) on a 30-year fixed loan; simple (undiscounted) break-even.
Refinance trigger: the weekly average 30-year rate at least 1.00 point below the borrower's note rate; closing costs and the borrower's own rate spread vs the survey average are ignored.
The no-point rate equals the survey rate in the start week; history is applied as point changes from that week's rate.
A hit means the refinance opportunity appeared; it does not assume the borrower took it or quantify how much of the point was lost.
limits: History, not a forecast. Overlapping weekly windows are not independent; weeks near 6.5-7.5% cluster in a few periods (1971-72, 1993-2002, 2006-08). The survey average is not any one borrower's rate. Moving or selling before break-even is not modeled.
